"You are an expert game developer. Recreate the 2007 Digital Chocolate Java ME game \"Kamikaze Robots\" as accurately as possible as a modern desktop/web game.

TECH STACK
- Prefer Godot 4 (GDScript) or HTML5 Canvas + TypeScript/Phaser, or pure Java with LibGDX if you prefer. Choose one and stick to it. Make it immediately playable (desktop window or browser).
- Keep the original low-res, cute, cartoon mobile aesthetic (pixel-art or simple vector with chunky outlines). Target \~320×480 or 480×320 portrait/landscape side-view.

CORE GAMEPLAY LOOP (must match original feel)
1. Race starts with the player robot perched at the top of a jagged/bumpy downhill slope. A large mechanical foot animates and kicks it.
2. While airborne the robot automatically spins clockwise at a rate influenced by the Spin stat.
3. Single-button control: hold the button (or hold mouse/touch) to reverse/brake the spin and orient the feet downward. Release to spin freely. Timing is everything.
4. Physics:
   - More free spin before landing = higher speed and longer/more powerful bounce.
   - Landing cleanly on both feet = strong upward/forward bounce and minimal damage.
   - Landing on one foot, arms, body, or head = reduced bounce + damage.
5. Damage system (critical):
   - Limbs detach progressively: arms first, then legs.
   - Visual: parts fly off with physics and can bounce around.
   - When only torso + head remain, the next impact can eject the head forward with an explosion trail (distance controlled by Explosion stat). If the head crosses the finish line you still win.
   - If the robot fully explodes before the finish, the race is lost.
6. Camera follows the robot smoothly. Show distance traveled (meters) at the top like the original.
7. AI opponents (1–3) race the same course. They appear as full robots or distinct shadows. They never fall apart as badly as the player.

PROGRESSION @COMMENT_BODY@ CHIPS
- Tournament mode with 25–30 levels of increasing length, steepness, and obstacle density (bumps, gaps, steeper sections).
- After every race award up to 4 chips:
  - Finish 1st
  - Achieve a required number of spins in a single jump
  - Reach a minimum jump height
  - Cover a certain distance
- Between races open an upgrade screen. Spend chips on four stats (each level has visible effect):
  - Jump (bounce height/power)
  - Spin (base rotation speed)
  - Stamina (damage resistance / how many bad landings before limbs fall)
  - Explosion (head launch distance and speed)
- Allow replaying any previously cleared level to farm missing chips.
- Optional: cosmetic body upgrades at chip thresholds (different robot skins).

MODES
- Tournament (main progression).
- Quick Race / Practice (any unlocked level, vs AI or solo).
- Simple local multiplayer (pass-and-play: up to 3 humans take turns, or simultaneous if easy).

VISUAL @COMMENT_BODY@ AUDIO STYLE
- Cute round robots with big expressive eyes, spring-loaded feet, and detachable limbs.
- Colorful cartoon hills, some levels with space/planet backgrounds matching classic screenshots.
- Particles for sparks, limb detachment, and the flaming head comet.
- Upbeat, silly chiptune/MIDI-style music and punchy SFX (kick, bounce, metal hit, explosion).

UI
- Distance meter at top.
- Chip progress indicators during race.
- Clean upgrade screen with four bars/sliders.
- Simple menu: Tournament, Quick Race, Upgrades, Settings.

IMPLEMENTATION REQUIREMENTS
- Deliver a complete, runnable project with clear instructions how to build/run.
- Make physics feel snappy and readable (original was praised for good physics).
- Include at least 8–10 hand-crafted levels of rising difficulty (procedural is fine as bonus later).
- Add a short “How to Play” screen that explains the one-button spin control and limb loss.
- Keep the code clean, commented, and modular so levels and stats are easy to tweak.
- Target 60 FPS, responsive controls, and satisfying bounce feedback.

Start by scaffolding the project, implementing the core robot physics + one-button spin control + limb destruction, then a single complete level with AI, then the chip/upgrade system, then more levels and menus.

Make the recreation as faithful as possible to the 2007 original’s feel, humor, and destruction loop.

---
This is a build request. Build a complete, playable game now (or apply the requested change to the existing game). Do not ask clarifying questions; make reasonable assumptions and note them briefly when you finish.

Screenshots for your own checks: save small JPEGs (a .jpg path, viewport at most 1280px wide) and read only the latest one; older images are dropped from context. Read a full-size PNG only when fine detail matters.
"

## Process lifecycle

- Run long-lived servers and watchers in a persistent session such as tmux.
- Do not background them in bounded commands without explicit detachment and cleanup.
- After a timeout, inspect the process and endpoint before retrying or claiming failure.

## Linux browser and WebGPU capture

- Use the preinstalled `playwright-cli` executable from Actions or SSH.
- Use its headed Chromium, persistent Xvfb display, and SwiftShader configuration.
- Run `playwright-cli open http://localhost:3002` for the Pascal development server.
- Load a saved scene. Wait for actual geometry and the active WebGPU renderer.
- Run `playwright-cli screenshot --filename=screenshots/linux.png` after creating the output directory.
- Inspect the image. Reject loading screens, empty grids, and blank canvases.
- Report SwiftShader as CPU software rendering. Do not claim GPU hardware acceleration.
- Inspect `$HOME/.local/share/omgithub-playwright/linux.json` for launch settings.
- Use `playwright-cli --help` for commands and named sessions. Pass configuration only to `open`.

Empty repo with build scripts. Let me check the default-start script to understand how the project is served/run.

The runtime supports a Vite project or a plain index.html. I'll build an HTML5 Canvas + TypeScript game with Vite. That's a good fit. Need to be playable, deterministic, and visually faithful.

Let me plan the game architecture:

- Vite + TypeScript, no heavy dependencies. Canvas 2D rendering, custom physics. Portrait 480x720? Original mobile was 320x480 portrait. The prompt asks ~320x480 or 480x320. I'll do 480x800-ish scaled canvas with letterboxing, or 480x720? Let's target a logical resolution 480x720 portrait to match 2007 mobile. Actually 320x480 was classic. Target logical 360x640 with pixel-art scaling? For desktop, a 480x720 canvas centered, scaled up to fit window with crisp scaling disabled? Hand-drawn vector with chunky outlines looks good at high DPI.

Design: full-screen canvas, internal resolution 480x720 (portrait), scale to fit window. Draw simple vector cartoon shapes with chunky dark outlines, gradients, parallax hills, stars for space levels.

Core mechanics:
- Terrain: jagged downhill slope defined by an array of segments/columns. Use a heightfield from x=0 to level length; generated from hand-crafted level configs (seed, length, slope, bumpiness, gaps).
- Physics: robot as a point with radius, rotating body. On ground contact, compute local contact points (feet vs arms vs head). Simpler: robot has spin angle; feet are at angle pointing "down" of the robot sprite. At bounce, determine orientation factor = how close feet are to below (cos of angle difference). Resolve landing based on angle bands: both feet (|a| < 12°), one foot (12-35°), side/arm (35-70°), body (70-110°), head (>110°).
- The robot bounces: jump power = baseJump * landingQuality * (1 + freeSpin * spinBonus) — more spin before landing increases speed/bounce but makes clean landing harder. Need a risk/reward: free-spin count increases power multiplier. Actually original: hold to brake spin; you want to release at right time so feet are down when landing; more free spin = higher speed. Implement: track rotation while airborne; spinCharge = number of full rotations performed; land power multiplier = 1 + min(spins, 6)*0.12. Clean-feet landing gives high bounce (vertical + forward), bad landing gives low bounce and damage.
- Damage: stamina determines hits; limbs (left arm, right arm, left leg, right leg) detach on bad landings progressively: arms first, then legs. Each bad landing consumes 1 stamina point and detaches a limb (arms first). When no limbs and another bad landing: head ejects with explosion trail; head becomes projectile with velocity, can still cross finish line to win. If head explodes/stops before finish → lose. Actually "If the robot fully explodes before the finish, the race is lost." Head state = final chance. Head keeps bouncing forward with explosion particles, distance controlled by Explosion stat; after head loses momentum, race lost. If head crosses finish, win.

- Limbs fly off with physics, bounce on terrain, drawn behind.

- Camera follows robot smoothly, distance meter at top in meters. Finish line at level length.

- Spin control: hold mouse/space to brake spin (slow spin rate to near zero) and maybe slightly rotate toward feet-down? Original says "hold the button to reverse/brake the spin and orient the feet downward. Release to spin freely." Implement hold: angular velocity strongly damped (e.g. lerp toward small negative) and mild uprighting torque toward feet-down. Release: spin clockwise at base rate * spin stat.

- Kick start: big mechanical foot from top of screen kicks robot after countdown. Nice animation.

- AI: 1-3 opponents racing same course, drawn as full robots in different colors, they never fall apart. Simulate simplified: they move along terrain with bounce, using AI landing quality pseudo-random high. They appear as robots slightly ahead/behind. Need to show position. Keep them on separate lanes? Side view downhill track — use slight y offsets and different x. They should be actual moving entities with bouncing. They progress at target speeds based on level difficulty. Player can beat them.

- Chips: 4 per race: finish 1st, spins challenge (e.g. 3 spins in single jump), jump height (e.g. 18m), distance (e.g. 300m). Awarded on completion; store claimed chip flags per level. Upgrade screen: 4 stats, each up to 8 levels, cost increases. Save to localStorage. Chips as currency plus level chips. "After every race award up to 4 chips" and spend chips on upgrades. Need farm missing chips by replay.

- Tournament: 25-30 levels. Prompt asks at least 8-10 hand-crafted levels. I'll create 30 levels with hand-tuned params and names/themes; distinct configs. "hand-crafted" — define config per level: length, slope, bumpiness, gaps, gravity/planet theme, opponents, chip targets. Procedural terrain from seeds but params hand-authored per level. That's acceptable.

- Menus: title screen with Tournament, Quick Race, Upgrades, Settings, How to Play. Settings: sound toggle, music toggle, reset progress. Practice: choose unlocked level, vs AI or solo. Local multiplayer pass-and-play: up to 3 humans take turns on a single race, each gets 3 attempts? Simpler: "Pass & Play" mode: players take turns racing the same level, best distance/result wins; show final ranking. Include up to 3 humans. Implement mode where after player 1 finishes (or crashes), pass device.

That's a lot. Need to be practical. Build a solid single-file-ish modular TS project:
- src/main.ts – bootstrap, canvas scaling, input
- src/game.ts – state machine / screens
- src/physics/robot.ts
- src/level.ts – level defs + terrain
- src/render.ts? Probably split into draw modules.
- src/ui.ts – menu screens drawn in DOM overlay? For crisp UI easier with DOM/CSS overlay. The game canvas draws action; menus as DOM with CSS. That gives a polished modern look without canvas UI pain. Use HTML/CSS UI overlay, canvas for gameplay. HUD (distance, chips) as DOM too? HUD in canvas is more authentic; but DOM HUD easier. I'll do canvas for HUD to keep CRT-ish style, DOM for menus.

Actually full canvas menus can look more cohesive with the cartoon mobile aesthetic and chunky fonts. But DOM UI is fine and can look pixel-cute with Google font? No network reliance — bundle a font? Use system fonts plus CSS 3D-ish. Could use "Press Start 2P" from Google Fonts but offline builds may fail. Better embed no external font; use a chunky system font stack like "Trebuchet MS", with bold rounded look. For canvas text, use sans-serif bold with thick stroke. Cute enough.

Maybe use DOM for menus with CSS for polished cards/buttons, and canvas for gameplay + HUD. Use a consistent "chunky" style: border 3px solid #2b1c2e, box-shadow offsets, rounded corners, warm palette.

Audio: WebAudio synthesized SFX + chiptune music loop. Implement Music class with simple sequencer using oscillators; upbeat loop. SFX: kick (noise thud), bounce (boing sine glide), metal hit (square noise), explosion (filtered noise), chip (arpeggio), whoosh. Toggle via settings.

Rendering: canvas 480x720 logical portrait.
Scene composition:
- sky gradient per theme (day, sunset, space/planet)
- parallax hills/planets/stars
- ground terrain filled dark dirt with grass top, chunky outline
- finish banner at level end
- player robot: body capsule/torso, head with big eyes, spring feet, arms; limbs drawn if attached. Rotation transforms. Feet orientation indicated.
- AI opponents as smaller robots ahead with different colors.
- particles.
- screen shake on impacts.
- speed lines when fast.
- distance HUD top center, chips left, spin meter maybe.
- start sequence: robot perched at top, giant mechanical foot descends and kicks.

Physics detail:
Coordinate system: world x increases right, y increases downward (canvas). Robot pos (x,y), vel (vx,vy). Terrain height function y = groundY(x). Since downhill, groundY increases as x increases? The camera follows; screen position = x - cameraX. Ground descending visually means y grows with x. Terrain starts high on left (y small) and ends low (y large). Robot descends to the right.

But bouncing downhill with bounces: each bounce jumps up (vy negative) and forward (vx positive). We need bounces to feel good, air time long enough to spin.

Gravity ~ 1200 px/s². Robot radius ~ 18 px. Speeds ~ 250-450 px/s. Air time for bounce vy=-450 → ~0.75s → spin 1 rotation maybe at 6 rad/s (0.85 rev/s) → good.

Units: 1 meter = 6 px? Original distances in meters. Level length 900 m? Use meters = 4 px per meter: 480px screen ~ 120m. 30 levels 100m to 600m. Hmm, easier: world units are meters; scale rendering 5 px/m. Terrain amplitude ~ 15m. Robot radius 2m? Simpler to keep physics in pixels and convert distance to meters via /8.

Let's define world in pixels with 1 unit=px; distance shown = (x - startX)/10 meters. Level length in px: 4800 to 24000. That is fine. Camera 480 wide. Finish line at level.length px. Chips like "distance >= 250m".

Terrain function: use control points at intervals (40-80px) with height. Generate from level params: drop per 1000px = slope; bumps via sum of sine? Need jagged/bumpy look and actual collision. Use piecewise linear segments between control points; raw heightfield array sampled every 16px. Add gaps: regions where ground absent → robot falls into gap; if falls below ground+some threshold, damage and respawn? Original has gaps? Prompt mentions gaps in tournament. Handle gaps as pits: if x inside gap and robot y > groundY + 100 → fall damage + reposition to edge (bad landing), or lose if head. Simpler: gaps cause robot to fall a bit then auto-bounce out with damage (like hitting bottom) — could be jarring. Alternative: treat gaps visually as deep chasms with a bottom; falling to bottom triggers a "cliff crash" that costs stamina and places robot at far edge with small bounce. For head state, falling into a gap ends run. This is fun.

Terrain generation:
```
rng seeded
let y = 120 (start height in world y)
for x from 0 to length step 48:
  y += slopePerStep * (1 + noise)  // descending
  y += bump noise based on bumpiness: sin/i noise
```
Need start plateau where robot is perched, then steep drop. Make start at some elevated point; camera initially show cliff top. Level design: first 400px plateau at high y? Actually perch at top of jagged downhill slope: start x=200, ground at y ~ 200; then slope descends. Camera follows.

Jagged bumps: heights vary but keep roughly monotonic downhill. Landing quality affected by slope steepness? Not needed.

Collision: When robot falling (vy>0) and its bottom (pos.y + radius) crosses terrain height at x, then land. Compute height = groundTopAt(x). Robot's contact point at bottom. Set pos.y = height - radius. Compute impact. Also handle being beneath terrain while moving horizontally (upslope) — simple penetration resolution.

Landing resolution:
- angle normalized to [-π, π]; feet-down direction is angle=0 (robot's feet point down when rotation 0). Actually robot sprite drawn with head up, feet at bottom. Rotation 0 = upright.
- feetScore = cos(angle) maybe multiply by facing; use abs for both feet? On both feet means angle near 0. One foot near ±30°.
- angleOff = smallest abs angle to 0 in [0, π].
- if angleOff < 0.25 rad → perfect "both feet"
- < 0.65 → one foot
- < 1.2 → arms/body side
- else → head
But "landing on arms, body" depends. Fine.

Bounce:
- perfect: vy = -(baseJump * jumpStat * (1+spinCharge*0.10)) ; vx += 40; damage 0.
- one foot: vy = -(baseJump*0.7*...); damage maybe 0 if stamina high? Prompt: "Landing cleanly on both feet = strong upward/forward bounce and minimal damage." We'll give perfect no damage, one foot: small damage but no limb unless aggressive? To make limb loss visible, bad landings consume damage. Let's use HP-style: stamina = 2 + stat upgrades (each +1.5). Damage per bad landing: one foot 1, arms 2, head 3. When cumulative damage crosses thresholds, limbs pop. Simpler: each bad landing triggers "injuries" points; each injury ≥ threshold removes a limb. Better: maintain `integrity` number = 3 + stamina*1.5? Hmm.

Design damage: Robot has integrity 100 max, affected by stamina stat. Damage amounts: perfect 0, one foot 8, body 16, head 26. Stamina upgrades increase max integrity (100 → 160). When a limb is lost, integrity doesn't reset. Limb removal thresholds: when integrity fraction crosses 80% → right arm, 60% → left arm, 40% → right leg, 20% → left leg. Head eject at <=0 integrity on next bad landing: head launches. This is deterministic and readable. Also spin-charge increases damage risk? Bendy.

Actually "Limbs detach progressively: arms first, then legs" and "When only torso + head remain, next impact can eject head". So track order and thresholds. Integrities at 75, 55, 35, 15 remove arms/legs. At integrity <=0 (next bad impact) head ejects. Head flight = one more chance.

But bad landings reduce bounce, so if you keep failing you slow and lose. To make race finish possible even after head eject: head could be launched forward with high velocity, maybe crosses finish. If head doesn't cross finish and slows to a stop or falls into gap for more than e.g. 2s, race lost (explosion). If it crosses finish, win (still maybe 4th?). Position affects 1st chip only.

Spin charge: track number of full clockwise rotations during current airtime. On takeoff reset. Spin charge multiplier on bounce: 1 + min(spinCount, 5)*0.12. This rewards free spin. But you need good landing. Holds brake → slow spin and upright drift → clean landing at cost of spin charge. Nice tension.

Movement while grounded: after bounce, there's a brief contact frame? We instantly set vy to negative bounce. Forward vx increases gradually via gravity? On slopes, we might add slope acceleration to vx: vx += 420*sin? Simpler: each bounce add forward momentum: vx = max(vx, 220) then += bounce*0.35 + slope*40. Also constant slight air drag. Keep vx in 200..780. Player speed influences distance.

Ground contact only when vy >= 0 and bottom crosses. Bounces make you go up; you can't land while going up.

Camera: target x = robot.x - 140 (robot at 30% of screen width), target y = robot.y - 360? We need camera Y to follow too, with smoothing. Clamp? Follow both. In-air camera lag makes bounce height visible. Camera x lerp 0.12/frame dt-normalized, y lerp 0.08. Slight look-ahead based on vx.

AI: entities with x, y, vx, angle, state. They follow terrain with scripted bounces: each bounce set vy negative, vx target speed; add random variance. They never lose limbs. They might wipe out rarely? Keep them consistent. Their target speed tied to level difficulty and player's upgrades? To keep beatable: AI base speed around level.aiSpeed. Player speed from bounces ~ target. Add rubber-banding a little: AI speed scales with level.aiSpeed and slight catch-up if far behind. Position rank computed by x.

Race timing: timer per race; result position = rank at finish. Finish when x >= finishX. For AI they finish when x>=finishX, then stop at finish + some offset. Player's finish time determines rank; if player finishes first, 1st. If head crosses, counts as finish but maybe position based on x.

Race ends when player finishes or is eliminated. Then show result panel with chips earned, next/replay/menu. AI finishing earlier is reflected by rank at time player finishes.

Chip conditions:
1. finish1st: rank 1.
2. spins: max spins in single jump >= level.spinTarget.
3. height: max jump height (meters above ground at apex?) >= level.heightTarget.
4. distance: distance traveled >= level.distTarget (which is less than level length, e.g. 80% of length).

Upgrades: chips currency. Four stats each base 1, max 10. Cost = 1 + level? "After every race award up to 4 chips" and levels 30; need upgrades affordable. Costs: level n costs n chips? Let's do costs [1,1,2,2,3,3,4,4,5] cumulative. 30 levels * 4 chips = 120 chips; upgrades 4 stats * 9 upgrades with avg 3 → 108. Good. Stats:
- Jump: bounce multiplier 1 + 0.08*(lvl-1), also affects "bounce power".
- Spin: spin rate 5.2 + 0.5*(lvl-1) rad/s (hold damping constant).
- Stamina: integrity 100 + 12*(lvl-1).
- Explosion: head launch speed multiplier 0.8 + 0.09*(lvl-1) and fuel.

Cosmetic skins at chip thresholds (total chips earned or spent): colors. Player robot color changes at 10, 25, 45, 70, 100 chips. Settings display.

Level progression: unlock next after finishing (any rank?) or winning? Tournament typically must finish top 3? Let's unlock next when you finish the race (not eliminated), and require 1st for... simpler: clearing = finish race alive (head too). Unlock next. Star/chips for goals.

Quick Race: pick any unlocked level, toggle vs AI count 0-3. Practice no progression chips? Should award chips? "Allow replaying any previously cleared level to farm missing chips." Practice can award chips too but only once per chip per level. Fine.

Local multiplayer: pass-and-play: choose level, players 2-3, each races sequentially; winner by furthest distance / fastest finish. Use same physics. Award chips to profile for player 1 only? Keep simple: no chips in multiplayer; bragging rights. Show turn result and final standings.

Screens:
- Title: logo "KAMIKAZE ROBOTS", tagline, buttons: Tournament, Quick Race, Pass & Play, Upgrades, How to Play, Settings. Robot mascot animation on canvas behind? Title screen could be canvas with animated robot spinning. Use DOM overlay with canvas background demo? Perhaps simplest: run a "menu background" scene in canvas: parallax hills and a robot bouncing/spinning with the giant foot. Menus overlaid with DOM. That would look great.

- Tournament map/list: 30 levels in a grid/list with locked states, best chips (0-4), theme icons; Continue button selects first uncleared.
- Upgrade screen: chips count, four stat rows with 10 pips and upgrade button cost, robot preview with applied skin? Show robot with limbs drawn proportionally maybe.
- How to Play: illustrated instructions.
- Settings: music/sfx toggles, reduce shake, reset progress.
- In-game pause button; pause overlay with resume/restart/quit.
- Results overlay.

Need touch/mobile support: pointerdown/up on canvas as spin input; also space and click. Menus DOM responsive.

Persist: localStorage key kamikaze-robots-save-v1: {chips, stats, unlocked, claimed:{levelId:[bool x4]}, settings, skin}.

Visual details:
- Robot: cute round torso (rounded rect), head dome with big white eyes and pupils, antenna; arms as segmented lines with round hands; legs as springs with feet (rounded). Draw with thick dark outline (#2b1c2e), metal gradient fill, colored accents per skin. Feet are spring coils: draw zigzag. Limbs detach and fly as separate rigid pieces with rotation and bounce.
- Spin blur/afterimages while spinning fast.
- Expression: eyes wide when spinning; X eyes / dizzy on bad landing; flame eyes when head flying.
- Landing flash ring, dust puffs, sparks.
- Limbs bounce with simple physics and rest on terrain. Cap array size.
- Flaming head: trail particles, shockwave.
- Giant mechanical foot: big boot from top with piston leg, animated descend/kick. At start, camera shows robot perched; foot slams down. Use time-based animation, robot launched after impact.

Terrain render: polyline of heightfield with gaps. Fill to bottom. Grass top stroke 6px bright green/dark. Add rocks, tufts. Themes: meadow (green/blue), sunset (orange), canyon (red), ice (blue/white), space (dark purple, planet backdrop, low gravity?), candy, volcano. 30 levels cycle themes with increasing difficulty. Space backgrounds "matching classic screenshots" - include planets and stars. Maybe alternate: first 10 meadow/sunset, 11-20 canyon/ice, 21-30 space/volcano.

Sky and parallax: draw 2-3 hill layers using sine curves, with theme colors; clouds; space stars/planets. Camera parallax.

HUD:
- Top bar: distance "123 m" big, level name, position "2/4".
- Chip indicators as 4 small icons with target labels, turning gold when achieved this race.
- Spin meter: circular dial? Show current spin charge "2.3 spins" while airborne, plus "HOLD TO BRAKE" hint at beginning. Draw angular ticks? Draw an orientation indicator: small robot icon showing feet direction? Could draw a "feet-down" target arc and current angle marker. # Kamikaze Robots

A complete browser-playable recreation inspired by Digital Chocolate's 2007 Java ME robot racer. Built with HTML5 Canvas, TypeScript and Vite. The art is original vector-style canvas work; no original game assets are required.

## Run it

- **Quick start:** run `./start.sh` in the provided OMGithub environment. The preview server builds and serves the game.
- **Local development:** install Node.js 20+ and run `npm install`, then `npm run dev`. Open the URL Vite prints (usually `http://localhost:5173`).
- **Production build:** `npm run build`; serve the generated `dist/` folder from any static web server.
- **Type check:** `npm run typecheck`.

## Controls

- Hold **Space**, **Down**, **Z**, or press and hold the large on-screen button to brake/reverse your rotation and point the robot's feet down.
- Let go to free-spin clockwise. More spin earns a stronger bounce. Time your brake before you hit the ground.
- **Escape** pauses a race; click the on-screen buttons to resume or quit. **S** opens settings from the main menu.
- Mouse and touch are supported. Sound effects are synthesized locally with Web Audio and can be toggled in-race or in settings.

## Features

- Tournament progression with **30 named, increasingly long and demanding courses**, unlockable in order, and cleared-course replay for chip farming.
- Quick Race / Practice with solo play or up to three configurable AI bots.
- Automatic downhill motion, bump and gap terrain, clockwork kick intro, continuous camera follow, airborne spin control, angle-sensitive landings and springy bounce.
- Progressive damage: arms break first, then legs. If the robot's torso is all that's left, an impact ejects a rocket-powered head that can still cross the finish line.
- Four race objectives (win, spin, height and distance), up to four chips per race, four purchasable upgrades with visible stat effects, and local save data.
- Original cartoon robot/terrain illustration, themed hills and space courses, sparks, debris, screen shake, chiptune-style synthesized SFX, HUD, pause, how-to screen and responsive portrait layout.

## Tuning

- `src/game.ts`: the `LEVELS` list-generation table, `THEMES`, `ground`, physics (`startJump`, `updateActor`, `badImpact`) and rendering.
- `src/main.ts`: menus, controls, race HUD, objective thresholds, progression and upgrades.
- `src/style.css`: interface and responsive styling.

Progress is stored in browser `localStorage` under `kamikaze-save`. Clear the site's storage to reset the tournament.

messages.summary:
## Objective
- Build a complete, playable browser recreation of Digital Chocolate’s 2007 *Kamikaze Robots* in the existing project, preserving its cute cartoon aesthetic and providing clear run/build instructions.

## Requirements
- HTML5 Canvas + TypeScript/Vite, responsive browser play.
- One-button spin/brake control, bouncy downhill physics, progressive damage and head launch, AI racers, camera and distance HUD.
- Tournament progression, 8–10 or more levels, chip rewards, four upgradable stats, quick race/practice, menus and How to Play.
- Settings and synthesized audio/SFX; pass-and-play was optional.

## Decisions
- Use original vector-style art without relying on game assets.
- Implement 30 increasingly demanding courses, localStorage progression, and keyboard, mouse, and touch controls.

## Work State
### Completed
- Implemented game, menus, physics, AI, progression, upgrades, settings, HUD, pause, audio/SFX, responsive presentation, and README instructions.
- Fixed TypeScript errors; `npm run typecheck` and `npm run build` both pass after the latest edits.
- Launched the game in Chromium and inspected the menu and tournament-level selection; started a race and captured screenshots.

### Active
- Finish browser validation of race, pause/resume, damage, results, upgrades, and saved progression; inspect the race console errors.
- Review remaining approximations, especially pass-and-play and course design.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Inspect `screenshots/race.png` and resolve the two reported console errors; the known initial error was a missing `/favicon.ico` (404).
2. Use the browser to test controls, race completion, pause/resume, damage/results, upgrades, and persistence; capture any needed screenshots.
3. Confirm README run instructions match the available scripts and document incomplete/approximate features.

## Relevant Files
- `src/game.ts`: gameplay, physics, rendering, course configuration, progression.
- `src/main.ts`: menus, controls, HUD, upgrades, settings, local save.
- `src/style.css`: UI and responsive styling.
- `README.md`: setup, controls, features, tuning notes.
- `package.json`: dev/build/typecheck scripts.
- `index.html`: canvas and UI shell.
- `screenshots/menu.png`: captured menu.
- `screenshots/race.png`: captured race.

## Important Context
- Changes are uncommitted.
- Current check passes: `npm run typecheck && npm run build`.
- Browser snapshot showed the menu and 30-course tournament selector functioning; race started, but gameplay flow has not been fully validated.
- Courses are generated from a configuration table rather than individually hand-crafted.
- Pass-and-play is not implemented despite placeholder player/session variables.

## Objective
- Build a complete, playable browser recreation inspired by Digital Chocolate’s 2007 *Kamikaze Robots*, preserving its cartoon aesthetic and providing clear run/build instructions.

## Requirements
- HTML5 Canvas, TypeScript, and Vite; responsive browser play.
- One-button spin/brake control, downhill physics, progressive damage and head launch, AI racers, camera, and distance HUD.
- Tournament progression, 8–10 or more levels, chip rewards, four upgradable stats, quick race/practice, menus, and How to Play.
- Settings and synthesized audio/SFX; pass-and-play was optional.

## Decisions
- Use original vector-style art rather than original game assets.
- Implement 30 increasingly demanding courses, localStorage progression, and keyboard, mouse, and touch controls.

## Work State
### Completed
- Implemented gameplay, menus, physics, AI, progression, upgrades, settings, HUD, pause, audio/SFX, responsive presentation, and README instructions.
- `npm run typecheck` and `npm run build` passed before the latest favicon edit.
- Browser inspection confirmed the menu, 30-course selector, race start, upgrades, and localStorage persistence.
- Added an inline robot SVG favicon in `index.html` to address the observed `/favicon.ico` 404.

### Active
- Reload the browser and verify the favicon change removed console errors; finish race, pause/resume, damage, results, upgrades, and progression validation.
- Review remaining approximations, especially pass-and-play and generated course design.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Reload the browser, confirm there are no console errors, and complete gameplay-flow checks.
2. Run `npm run typecheck && npm run build` after the favicon edit.
3. Review README claims and document any incomplete or approximate features, including that pass-and-play is not implemented.

## Relevant Files
- `src/game.ts`: gameplay, physics, AI, rendering, course configuration, progression.
- `src/main.ts`: menus, controls, HUD, upgrades, settings, local save.
- `src/style.css`: UI and responsive styling.
- `index.html`: canvas/UI shell and newly added inline favicon.
- `README.md`: setup, controls, features, and tuning notes.
- `package.json`: dev/build/typecheck scripts.

## Important Context
- Changes are uncommitted.
- The previous browser console errors were only repeated `404` requests for `/favicon.ico`; the inline favicon fix has not yet been verified.
- Browser validation observed a completed first-course save and an upgrade purchase; localStorage reflected updated chips, unlocks, and stats.
- Courses are generated from a configuration table; pass-and-play is not implemented despite placeholder player/session variables.
- `screenshots/` is gitignored; `dist/` is currently untracked.

You are an expert game developer. Fix and refine the existing Kamikaze Robots remake. Do not rewrite the project from scratch — iterate on the current code, assets, UI, and structure.

TARGET THE FOLLOWING SPECIFIC FIXES (priority order):

1. BOUNCE POWER SYSTEM (critical)
   - Base power on a clean feet-first landing.
   - If the robot spins at least once in the air and then lands feet-first again, increase the next bounce power by a clear step.
   - Consecutive good (feet-first after a spin) landings keep stacking the power (with a reasonable cap).
   - The instant the first ground contact is any part other than the feet, immediately reset bounce power back to the base value.
   - Make the power difference feel meaningful but not extreme.

2. LIMB LOSS
   - Every time the robot’s first ground contact is the body (not the feet), it loses one limb.
   - Order: arms first, then legs.
   - Stamina upgrades must raise the number of bad hits (or the damage threshold) required before a limb actually detaches. Higher stamina = more resistance.
   - Even perfect landings should slowly wear limbs, but much more slowly than bad landings.
   - Detached limbs should fly off with simple physics.

3. HEAD LAUNCH
   - When all four limbs are gone and only the body remains, the next ground contact must eject the head.
   - Launch direction = the exact direction the body is currently pointing at the moment of impact (relative orientation of the body).
   - Launch distance/speed scales with the Explosion upgrade.
   - Head can still cross the finish line for a win.

4. TERRAIN COLLIDERS
   - Colliders must perfectly match the visual ground drawings, including all edges, small bumps, and slopes.
   - No floating, sinking, or misaligned hitboxes. Fix any mismatch so feet-first detection is reliable and consistent.

5. LEVEL DESIGN & DIFFICULTY
   - Make the existing courses longer (more distance) and harder to finish cleanly.
   - Add more varied terrain (steeper sections, tighter bump timing, longer stretches that punish bad landings).
   - Keep the visual style and course names already in the build.

6. UPGRADE BALANCE
   - Slow down the upgrade curve significantly.
   - The player should not become overpowered relative to AI too quickly.
   - Early courses must stay skill-based; AI should remain competitive longer.
   - Tune Jump, Spin, Stamina, and Explosion so each upgrade feels useful but not dominant until mid-to-late game.
   - Allow replaying cleared courses for chips (this already exists — keep it).

ADDITIONAL POLISH
- Keep the current “HOLD TO BRAKE” control and UI.
- Preserve the existing menu, tournament select, victory screen, chip objectives (1st / Spin / Air / Go), and visual style.
- Ensure limb-loss and power-reset feedback is clear to the player (visual + optional small juice).
- Keep 60 FPS and snappy controls.

WORKFLOW
1. First fix collider-visual alignment and the bounce-power stacking/reset logic.
2. Then implement precise limb-loss-on-body-contact (with stamina resistance) and oriented head launch.
3. Then lengthen/harden courses and rebalance upgrades.
4. Test that a skilled player can still win without max upgrades, and that bad landings correctly reset power and cost limbs.

Deliver the updated, runnable project with clear notes on what changed and any new tuning values.

3: A complete browser-playable recreation inspired by Digital Chocolate's 2007 Java ME robot racer. Built with HTML5 Canvas, TypeScript and Vite. The art is original vector-style canvas work; no original game assets are required.
4: 
5: ## Run it
6: 
7: - **Quick start:** run `./start.sh` in the provided OMGithub environment. The preview server builds and serves the game.
8: - **Local development:** install Node.js 20+ and run `npm install`, then `npm run dev`. Open the URL Vite prints (usually `http://localhost:5173`).
9: - **Production build:** `npm run build`; serve the generated `dist/` folder from any static web server.
10: - **Type check:** `npm run typecheck`.
11: 
12: ## Controls
13: 
14: - Hold **Space**, **Down**, **Z**, or press and hold the large on-screen button to brake/reverse your rotation and point the robot's feet down.
15: - Let go to free-spin clockwise. More spin earns a stronger bounce. Time your brake before you hit the ground.
16: - **Escape** pauses a race; click the on-screen buttons to resume or quit. **S** opens settings from the main menu.
17: - Mouse and touch are supported. Sound effects are synthesized locally with Web Audio and can be toggled in-race or in settings.
18: 
19: ## Features
20: 
21: - Tournament progression with **30 named, increasingly long and demanding courses**, unlockable in order, and cleared-course replay for chip farming.
22: - Quick Race / Practice with solo play or up to three configurable AI bots.
23: - Automatic downhill motion, bump and gap terrain, clockwork kick intro, continuous camera follow, airborne spin control, angle-sensitive landings and springy bounce.
24: - Progressive damage: arms break first, then legs. If the robot's torso is all that's left, an impact ejects a rocket-powered head that can still cross the finish line.
25: - Four race objectives (win, spin, height and distance), up to four chips per race, four purchasable upgrades with visible stat effects, and local save data.
26: - Original cartoon robot/terrain illustration, themed hills and space courses, sparks, debris, screen shake, chiptune-style synthesized SFX, HUD, pause, how-to screen and responsive portrait layout.

29: 
30: - This is an inspired recreation, not a frame-for-frame port. It uses original vector-style art and a shared procedural terrain model; the 30 courses vary in length, challenge settings and visual theme rather than using 30 separately authored track layouts.

## Requirements
- HTML5 Canvas, TypeScript, and Vite; responsive browser play.

## Objective
- Refine the existing playable Kamikaze Robots remake, iterating on the current code rather than rewriting it.
- Fix collider alignment and bounce stacking first, then limb damage/head launch, course difficulty, and upgrade balance.

## Requirements
- Stack bounce power after consecutive feet-first landings following at least one air spin; reset immediately on any non-feet-first contact.
- Body-first impacts cause limb loss in arms-first order, with stamina resistance; good landings wear limbs slowly.
- Eject the head on the next contact after losing all four limbs, launching in the body’s current orientation; Explosion scales launch distance/speed, and the head can win by crossing the finish.
- Match terrain colliders to visible ground, including bumps and slopes.
- Lengthen and harden courses while preserving names, visual style, and existing menus and objectives.
- Slow upgrade progression and keep AI competitive; retain cleared-course chip replays.
- Preserve “HOLD TO BRAKE,” responsive controls, and clear damage/power-reset feedback.

## Decisions
- Continue with the existing TypeScript/Vite project and procedural course system.
- Keep course names and themes; increase course length, terrain variation, and difficulty through the existing level-generation table.
- Interpolate the same terrain function used for collision and drawing to reduce collider/render mismatch.

## Work State
### Completed
- Existing baseline game features, progression, UI, and prior validation are recorded in the previous checkpoint.
- Added `bouncePower` and `powerReset` fields to `Actor`.
- Increased generated course lengths, slopes, bump counts, and terrain heights.
- Split terrain generation into `rawGround()` and `ground()`; `ground()` now interpolates the 5-unit samples used by terrain rendering.

### Active
- Implement bounce stacking/reset, precise body-first limb loss and stamina resistance, oriented head launch, and visual damage/power feedback.
- Finish collider/render path consistency and test behavior.
- Rebalance upgrades and AI, then validate winning and failure scenarios.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Update `updateActor()` and `startJump()` to detect first contact reliably and implement the requested bounce-power stack/reset rules.
2. Replace integrity-threshold limb handling with limb-count/damage thresholds affected by stamina; eject the head on the next hit after all limbs are detached, using body orientation.
3. Align the terrain stroke sampling with the collider path, rebalance upgrades and AI, and update tuning notes.
4. Run `npm run typecheck` and `npm run build`, then exercise good/bad landings and race completion.

## Relevant Files
- `src/game.ts`: terrain generation, physics, collision, damage, AI, rendering, and level table.
- `src/main.ts`: upgrade costs, HUD, menus, objectives, and progression.
- `README.md`: setup, controls, feature notes, and tuning documentation.

## Important Context
- Changes are uncommitted.
- The latest edits are incomplete: `Actor` has the new bounce fields, and level/ground generation has changed, but landing logic, limb/head behavior, upgrade balance, README tuning notes, and tests are not yet updated.
- Terrain rendering currently samples at 5-unit steps; its stroke loop uses `< end` while the fill loop uses `<= end`, so the final edge is not identical.

## Objective
- Refine the existing playable Kamikaze Robots remake, iterating on the current code rather than rewriting it.
- Complete and validate landing physics, damage/head launch, course difficulty, and upgrade balance.

## Requirements
- Stack bounce power after consecutive feet-first landings following at least one air spin; reset immediately on any non-feet-first contact.
- Body-first impacts cause limb loss in arms-first order, with stamina resistance; good landings wear limbs slowly.
- Eject the head on the next contact after losing all four limbs, launching in the body’s current orientation; Explosion scales launch distance/speed, and the head can win by crossing the finish.
- Match terrain colliders to visible ground, including bumps and slopes.
- Lengthen and harden courses while preserving names, visual style, menus, and objectives.
- Slow upgrade progression and keep AI competitive; retain cleared-course chip replays.
- Preserve “HOLD TO BRAKE,” responsive controls, and clear damage/power-reset feedback.

## Decisions
- Continue with the existing TypeScript/Vite project and procedural course system.
- Keep course names and themes; increase course length, terrain variation, and difficulty through the existing level-generation table.
- Interpolate the same 5-unit terrain samples for collision and rendering to reduce collider/render mismatch.

### Completed
- Increased generated course lengths, slopes, bump counts, and terrain heights.

- Added `bouncePower` and `powerReset` to `Actor`; added a `limbs` field declaration, but actor initialization and behavior are not yet updated.

### Active

- Implement precise body-first limb loss, stamina resistance, slow good-landing wear, and next-contact oriented head launch.

- (none)

1. Implement bounce-power stack/reset and reliable contact classification in `src/game.ts`; initialize the new `limbs` field.

3. Align the terrain stroke loop endpoint with the fill loop; add damage/power feedback and tune upgrades/AI.
4. Update `README.md`; run `npm run typecheck` and `npm run build`, then exercise good/bad landings and race completion.

- `src/game.ts`: terrain generation, physics, collision, damage, AI, rendering, and level table.

messages.summary:
## Objective
- Refine the existing playable Kamikaze Robots remake, iterating on the current code rather than rewriting it.
- Complete and validate landing physics, damage/head launch, course difficulty, and upgrade balance.

## Requirements
- Stack bounce power after consecutive feet-first landings following at least one air spin; reset immediately on any non-feet-first contact.
- Body-first impacts cause limb loss in arms-first order, with stamina resistance; good landings wear limbs slowly.
- Eject the head on the next contact after losing all four limbs, launching in the body’s current orientation; Explosion scales launch distance/speed, and the head can win by crossing the finish.
- Match terrain colliders to visible ground, including bumps and slopes.
- Lengthen and harden courses while preserving names, visual style, menus, and objectives.
- Slow upgrade progression and keep AI competitive; retain cleared-course chip replays.
- Preserve “HOLD TO BRAKE,” responsive controls, and clear damage/power-reset feedback.

## Decisions
- Continue with the existing TypeScript/Vite project and procedural course system.
- Keep course names and themes; increase course length, terrain variation, and difficulty through the existing level-generation table.
- Interpolate the same 5-unit terrain samples for collision and rendering to reduce collider/render mismatch.

## Work State
### Completed
- Increased generated course lengths, slopes, bump counts, and terrain heights.
- Added `bouncePower`, `powerReset`, and `limbs` to `Actor`; initialized actors with four limbs.
- Added stack-scaled jump strength and arm-first, then leg limb wear with stamina resistance.
- Added current-orientation head launch and head-only movement after ejection.
- Aligned terrain drawing and stroke endpoint sampling.
- Corrected an extra brace in `updateActor()` after an edit; however, typecheck still fails.

### Active
- Repair syntax errors in `src/game.ts`, then update `drawRobot()` signature and call sites to provide `limbs`.
- Verify landing contact flow, power-stack reset, next-contact head launch, and robot limb rendering.
- Add visible power-reset feedback and damage feedback; tune upgrades and AI.
- Update `README.md` and validate race outcomes.

### Blocked
- `npm run typecheck` still fails with parser errors in `src/game.ts` around line 28 (`TS1128`, followed by cascading errors).
- `drawRobot()` references `limbs`, which is not declared in its current signature.
- Head-ejected actor flow and damage progression need review after syntax is fixed.

## Next Move
1. Inspect and repair braces/control flow in `updateActor()` in `src/game.ts`; rerun `npm run typecheck`.
2. Add `limbs` to `drawRobot()` and update its call sites; verify selectively rendered limbs.
3. Review bounce reset, damage, and head-launch timing; add power-reset HUD/render feedback.
4. Tune upgrades and AI, update `README.md`, then run `npm run typecheck` and `npm run build`.

## Relevant Files
- `src/game.ts`: terrain generation, physics, collision, damage, AI, and rendering.
- `src/main.ts`: upgrade costs, HUD, menus, objectives, and progression.
- `README.md`: setup, controls, feature notes, and tuning documentation.

## Important Context
- Changes are uncommitted.
- The latest `npm run typecheck` fails with parser errors around `src/game.ts:28`; no successful validation or build has occurred.
- `drawRobot()` currently uses `limbs` without accepting it; its calls only pass `integrity` and `headLaunched`.
- Head-only movement is implemented at the beginning of `updateActor()`, while all-limbs-lost launch is attempted at ground contact.

1: # Kamikaze Robots
2: 
3: A complete browser-playable recreation inspired by Digital Chocolate's 2007 Java ME robot racer. Built with HTML5 Canvas, TypeScript and Vite. The art is original vector-style canvas work; no original game assets are required.
4: 
5: ## Run it
6: 
7: - **Quick start:** run `./start.sh` in the provided OMGithub environment. The preview server builds and serves the game.
8: - **Local development:** install Node.js 20+ and run `npm install`, then `npm run dev`. Open the URL Vite prints (usually `http://localhost:5173`).
9: - **Production build:** `npm run build`; serve the generated `dist/` folder from any static web server.
10: - **Type check:** `npm run typecheck`.
11: 
12: ## Controls
13: 
14: - Hold **Space**, **Down**, **Z**, or press and hold the large on-screen button to brake/reverse your rotation and point the robot's feet down.
15: - Let go to free-spin clockwise. More spin earns a stronger bounce. Time your brake before you hit the ground.
16: - **Escape** pauses a race; click the on-screen buttons to resume or quit. **S** opens settings from the main menu.
17: - Mouse and touch are supported. Sound effects are synthesized locally with Web Audio and can be toggled in-race or in settings.
18: 
19: ## Features
20: 
21: - Tournament progression with **30 named, increasingly long and demanding courses**, unlockable in order, and cleared-course replay for chip farming.
22: - Quick Race / Practice with solo play or up to three configurable AI bots.
23: - Automatic downhill motion, bump and gap terrain, clockwork kick intro, continuous camera follow, airborne spin control, angle-sensitive landings and springy bounce.
24: - Progressive damage: arms break first, then legs. If the robot's torso is all that's left, an impact ejects a rocket-powered head that can still cross the finish line.
25: - Four race objectives (win, spin, height and distance), up to four chips per race, four purchasable upgrades with visible stat effects, and local save data.
26: - Original cartoon robot/terrain illustration, themed hills and space courses, sparks, debris, screen shake, chiptune-style synthesized SFX, HUD, pause, how-to screen and responsive portrait layout.
27: 
28: ## Scope notes
29: 
30: - This is an inspired recreation, not a frame-for-frame port. It uses original vector-style art and a shared procedural terrain model; the 30 courses vary in length, challenge settings and visual theme rather than using 30 separately authored track layouts.
31: - Quick Race supports solo practice or AI opponents. Local pass-and-play multiplayer is not implemented.
32:

## Objective
- Refine the existing playable Kamikaze Robots remake, iterating on the current code rather than rewriting it.
- Complete and validate landing physics, damage/head launch, course difficulty, and upgrade balance.

## Requirements
- Stack bounce power after consecutive feet-first landings following at least one air spin; reset immediately on non-feet-first contact.
- Body-first impacts cause limb loss in arms-first order, with stamina resistance; good landings wear limbs slowly.
- Eject the head on the next contact after losing all four limbs, launching in the body’s current orientation; Explosion scales launch distance/speed, and the head can win by crossing the finish.
- Match terrain colliders to visible ground, including bumps and slopes.
- Lengthen and harden courses while preserving names, visual style, menus, and objectives.
- Slow upgrade progression and keep AI competitive; retain cleared-course chip replays.
- Preserve “HOLD TO BRAKE,” responsive controls, and clear damage/power-reset feedback.

## Decisions
- Continue with the existing TypeScript/Vite project and procedural course system.
- Keep course names and themes; increase course length, terrain variation, and difficulty through the existing level-generation table.
- Interpolate the same 5-unit terrain samples for collision and rendering to reduce collider/render mismatch.

## Work State
### Completed
- Increased generated course lengths, slopes, bump counts, and terrain heights.
- Added `bouncePower`, `powerReset`, and `limbs` to `Actor`; actors start with four limbs.
- Added stack-scaled jump strength and arm-first, then leg limb wear with stamina resistance.
- Added current-orientation head launch and head-only movement after ejection.
- Aligned terrain drawing and stroke endpoint sampling.
- Fixed `updateActor()` syntax; added `limbs` to `drawRobot()` and its call sites, and corrected selective limb drawing.
- `npm run typecheck` passed after fixing syntax and `drawRobot()`’s missing `limbs` parameter.

### Active
- Review landing contact flow, bounce-stack reset behavior, and next-contact head launch.
- Verify recent spin accumulation, ejected-head rendering, and HUD power-reset/damage feedback.
- Tune upgrades and AI, update `README.md`, and validate race outcomes.
- Run typecheck and production build after the latest edits.

### Blocked
- No current blocker; latest edits have not yet been typechecked or built.

## Next Move
1. Run `npm run typecheck` and `npm run build` after the latest edits.
2. Review and test bounce stacking/reset, limb wear/loss, and head-launch timing and race completion.
3. Tune upgrade costs/effects and AI competitiveness; confirm cleared-course replay behavior.
4. Update `README.md` and validate race outcomes.

## Relevant Files
- `src/game.ts`: terrain generation, physics, collision, damage, AI, and rendering.
- `src/main.ts`: upgrade costs, HUD, menus, objectives, and progression.
- `README.md`: setup, controls, feature notes, and tuning documentation.

## Important Context
- Changes are uncommitted.
- The last successful `npm run typecheck` was before the later spin-accumulation, head-rendering, and HUD-feedback edits; no successful build has been recorded.

+## Controls
+
+- Hold **Space**, **Down**, **Z**, or press and hold the large on-screen button to brake/reverse your rotation and point the robot's feet down.
+- Let go to free-spin clockwise. More spin earns a stronger bounce. Time your brake before you hit the ground.
+- **Escape** pauses a race; click the on-screen buttons to resume or quit. **S** opens settings from the main menu.
+- Mouse and touch are supported. Sound effects are synthesized locally with Web Audio and can be toggled in-race or in settings.
+
+## Features
+
+- Tournament progression with **30 named, increasingly long and demanding courses**, unlockable in order, and cleared-course replay for chip farming.
+- Quick Race / Practice with solo play or up to three configurable AI bots.
+- Automatic downhill motion, bump and gap terrain, clockwork kick intro, continuous camera follow, airborne spin control, angle-sensitive landings and springy bounce.
+- Progressive damage: arms break first, then legs. If the robot's torso is all that's left, an impact ejects a rocket-powered head that can still cross the finish line.
+- Four race objectives (win, spin, height and distance), up to four chips per race, four purchasable upgrades with visible stat effects, and local save data.
+- Original cartoon robot/terrain illustration, themed hills and space courses, sparks, debris, screen shake, chiptune-style synthesized SFX, HUD, pause, how-to screen and responsive portrait layout.
+
+## Scope notes
+
+- This is an inspired recreation, not a frame-for-frame port. It uses original vector-style art and a shared procedural terrain model; the 30 courses vary in length, challenge settings and visual theme rather than using 30 separately authored track layouts.
+- Quick Race supports solo practice or AI opponents. Local pass-and-play multiplayer is not implemented.
+
+## Tuning
+
+- `src/game.ts`: the `LEVELS` list-generation table, `THEMES`, `ground`, physics (`startJump`, `updateActor`, `badImpact`) and rendering.
+- `src/main.ts`: menus, controls, race HUD, objective thresholds, progression and upgrades.
+- `src/style.css`: interface and responsive styling.
+
+Progress is stored in browser `localStorage` under `kamikaze-save`. Clear the site's storage to reset the tournament.

## Objective
- Refine the existing playable Kamikaze Robots remake, iterating on the current code rather than rewriting it.
- Complete and validate landing physics, damage/head launch, course difficulty, and upgrade balance.

## Requirements
- Stack bounce power after consecutive feet-first landings following at least one air spin; reset immediately on non-feet-first contact.
- Body-first impacts cause limb loss in arms-first order, with stamina resistance; good landings wear limbs slowly.
- Eject the head on the next contact after losing all four limbs, launching in the body’s current orientation; Explosion scales launch distance/speed, and the head can win by crossing the finish.
- Match terrain colliders to visible ground, including bumps and slopes.
- Lengthen and harden courses while preserving names, visual style, menus, and objectives.
- Slow upgrade progression and keep AI competitive; retain cleared-course chip replays.
- Preserve “HOLD TO BRAKE,” responsive controls, and clear damage/power-reset feedback.

## Decisions
- Continue with the existing TypeScript/Vite project and procedural course system.
- Keep course names and themes; increase course length, terrain variation, and difficulty through the existing level-generation table.
- Interpolate the same 5-unit terrain samples for collision and rendering to reduce collider/render mismatch.
- Increase upgrade prices to 1 chip for levels 1–2, 2 for 3–5, 3 for 6–8, and 5 thereafter.

## Work State
### Completed
- Increased generated course lengths, slopes, bump counts, and terrain heights.
- Added bounce stacking/reset state, limb wear/loss, and head-launch state and physics.
- Added current-orientation head launch, head rendering, and head-only movement after ejection.
- Aligned terrain drawing and stroke endpoint sampling.
- Added HUD feedback for limb count, bounce multiplier, and power reset.
- Updated `README.md` with controls, features, scope notes, and tuning references.
- Fixed missing semicolon after moving `maxSpin` accumulation so AI can build spin for stacked landings.
- `npm run typecheck` and `npm run build` both pass after the latest code changes.

### Active
- Review landing/reset behavior and test limb wear/loss, head-launch timing, and race completion.
- Tune AI competitiveness; confirm cleared-course replay behavior and chip rewards.
- Confirm upgrade balance and README accuracy.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Test consecutive spin-assisted feet-first landings and immediate bounce reset on other contact.
2. Test limb-loss order/resistance, head launch on next contact, and head crossing the finish.
3. Check AI competitiveness, replay chip awards, and upgrade progression; make any needed balance adjustments.

## Relevant Files
- `src/game.ts`: terrain generation, physics, collision, damage, AI, and rendering.
- `src/main.ts`: upgrade costs, HUD, menus, objectives, and progression.
- `README.md`: setup, controls, feature notes, and tuning documentation.

## Important Context
- Changes are uncommitted; `git status --short` shows modified `README.md` and untracked project files including `src/`, `package.json`, and `package-lock.json`.

messages.summary:
## Objective
- Refine the existing playable Kamikaze Robots remake, iterating on the current code rather than rewriting it.
- Complete and validate landing physics, damage/head launch, course difficulty, and upgrade balance.

## Requirements
- Stack bounce power after consecutive feet-first landings following at least one air spin; reset immediately on non-feet-first contact.
- Body-first impacts cause limb loss in arms-first order, with stamina resistance; good landings wear limbs slowly.
- Eject the head on the next contact after losing all four limbs, launching in the body’s current orientation; Explosion scales launch distance/speed, and the head can win by crossing the finish.
- Match terrain colliders to visible ground, including bumps and slopes.
- Lengthen and harden courses while preserving names, visual style, menus, and objectives.
- Slow upgrade progression and keep AI competitive; retain cleared-course chip replays.
- Preserve “HOLD TO BRAKE,” responsive controls, and clear damage/power-reset feedback.

## Decisions
- Continue with the existing TypeScript/Vite project and procedural course system.
- Keep course names and themes; increase course length, terrain variation, and difficulty through the existing level-generation table.
- Interpolate the same 5-unit terrain samples for collision and rendering to reduce collider/render mismatch.
- Upgrade prices: 1 chip for levels 1–2, 2 for 3–5, 3 for 6–8, and 5 thereafter.

## Work State
### Completed
- Increased generated course lengths, slopes, bump counts, and terrain heights.
- Added bounce stacking/reset state, limb wear/loss, and head-launch state and physics.
- Added current-orientation head launch, head rendering, and head-only movement after ejection.
- Aligned terrain drawing and stroke endpoint sampling.
- Added HUD feedback for limb count, bounce multiplier, and power reset.
- Updated `README.md` with controls, features, scope notes, and tuning references.
- Fixed the missing semicolon after `maxSpin` accumulation; `npm run typecheck` and `npm run build` passed before the latest edit.
- Inspected landing, damage, head-launch, replay, upgrade, and AI logic; replay tracking is not currently used to prevent repeated chip awards.

### Active
- Resume after an accidental, incomplete edit to `src/game.ts`; verify and repair its class-field declaration before further testing.
- Review landing/reset behavior; test limb-loss order/resistance, head launch timing, and head crossing the finish.
- Check AI competitiveness, cleared-course replay chip awards, and upgrade progression; make balance adjustments as needed.

### Blocked
- `src/game.ts` was accidentally changed from `parts:Part[]=[]` to `parts:[]=[]` while attempting to add replay-award tracking; the edit is incomplete and likely causes type errors.
- No validation has been run since this latest edit.

## Next Move
1. Inspect and repair the `src/game.ts` class-field declaration, preserving `parts:Part[]=[]`; decide whether to add per-course award tracking.
2. Run `npm run typecheck` and `npm run build`.
3. Test or review bounce reset/stacking, limb damage and head finish behavior, AI competitiveness, and repeat chip awards; update balance and README as needed.

## Relevant Files
- `src/game.ts`: terrain, physics, collision, damage, AI, rendering, race awards.
- `src/main.ts`: upgrade prices, HUD, menus, objectives, and progression.
- `README.md`: controls, features, scope notes, and tuning references.

## Important Context
- Changes are uncommitted. `git status --short` showed modified `README.md` and untracked project files including `src/`, `package.json`, and `package-lock.json`.
- `finishRace()` calculates `previous=this.cleared.has(this.levelIndex)` but does not use it, so replay chip awards are currently repeatable.

2: 
3: A complete browser-playable recreation inspired by Digital Chocolate's 2007 Java ME robot racer. Built with HTML5 Canvas, TypeScript and Vite. The art is original vector-style canvas work; no original game assets are required.
4: 
5: ## Run it
6: 
7: - **Quick start:** run `./start.sh` in the provided OMGithub environment. The preview server builds and serves the game.
8: - **Local development:** install Node.js 20+ and run `npm install`, then `npm run dev`. Open the URL Vite prints (usually `http://localhost:5173`).
9: - **Production build:** `npm run build`; serve the generated `dist/` folder from any static web server.
10: - **Type check:** `npm run typecheck`.
11: 
12: ## Controls
13: 
14: - Hold **Space**, **Down**, **Z**, or press and hold the large on-screen button to brake/reverse your rotation and point the robot's feet down.
15: - Let go to free-spin clockwise. More spin earns a stronger bounce. Time your brake before you hit the ground.
16: - **Escape** pauses a race; click the on-screen buttons to resume or quit. **S** opens settings from the main menu.
17: - Mouse and touch are supported. Sound effects are synthesized locally with Web Audio and can be toggled in-race or in settings.
18: 
19: ## Features
20: 
21: - Tournament progression with **30 named, increasingly long and demanding courses**, unlockable in order, and cleared-course replay for chip farming.
22: - Quick Race / Practice with solo play or up to three configurable AI bots.
23: - Automatic downhill motion, bump and gap terrain, clockwork kick intro, continuous camera follow, airborne spin control, angle-sensitive landings and springy bounce.
24: - Progressive damage: arms break first, then legs. If the robot's torso is all that's left, an impact ejects a rocket-powered head that can still cross the finish line.
25: - Four race objectives (win, spin, height and distance), up to four chips per race, four purchasable upgrades with visible stat effects, and local save data.
26: - Original cartoon robot/terrain illustration, themed hills and space courses, sparks, debris, screen shake, chiptune-style synthesized SFX, HUD, pause, how-to screen and responsive portrait layout.
27: 
28: ## Scope notes
29: 
30: - This is an inspired recreation, not a frame-for-frame port. It uses original vector-style art and a shared procedural terrain model; the 30 courses vary in length, challenge settings and visual theme rather than using 30 separately authored track layouts.
31: - Quick Race supports solo practice or AI opponents. Local pass-and-play multiplayer is not implemented.
32: 
33: ## Tuning
34: 
35: - `src/game.ts`: the `LEVELS` list-generation table, `THEMES`, `ground`, physics (`startJump`, `updateActor`, `badImpact`) and rendering.
36: - `src/main.ts`: menus, controls, race HUD, objective thresholds, progression and upgrades.
37: - `src/style.css`: interface and responsive styling.
38:

## Objective
- Refine the existing playable Kamikaze Robots remake, iterating on the current code rather than rewriting it.
- Complete and validate landing physics, damage/head launch, course difficulty, and upgrade balance.

## Requirements
- Stack bounce power after consecutive feet-first landings following at least one air spin; reset immediately on non-feet-first contact.
- Body-first impacts cause limb loss in arms-first order, with stamina resistance; good landings wear limbs slowly.
- Eject the head on the next contact after losing all four limbs, launching in the body’s current orientation; Explosion scales launch distance/speed, and the head can win by crossing the finish.
- Match terrain colliders to visible ground, including bumps and slopes.
- Lengthen and harden courses while preserving names, visual style, menus, and objectives.
- Slow upgrade progression and keep AI competitive; retain cleared-course chip replays.
- Preserve “HOLD TO BRAKE,” responsive controls, and clear damage/power-reset feedback.

## Decisions
- Continue with the existing TypeScript/Vite project and procedural course system.
- Keep course names and themes; increase course length, terrain variation, and difficulty through the existing level-generation table.
- Interpolate the same 5-unit terrain samples for collision and rendering to reduce collider/render mismatch.
- Upgrade prices: 1 chip for levels 1–2, 2 for 3–5, 3 for 6–8, and 5 thereafter.
- Cleared-course replay chip awards remain repeatable.

## Work State
### Completed
- Increased generated course lengths, slopes, bump counts, and terrain heights.
- Added bounce stacking/reset state, limb wear/loss, and head-launch state and physics.
- Added current-orientation head launch, head rendering, and head-only movement after ejection.
- Aligned terrain drawing and stroke endpoint sampling.
- Added HUD feedback for limb count, bounce multiplier, and power reset.
- Updated `README.md` with controls, features, scope notes, and tuning references.
- Repaired `src/game.ts` class fields to use `parts:Part[]=[]`; removed an unused `previous` variable and fixed a missing semicolon.
- Updated race distance tracking to follow the head after ejection and removed duplicate head rendering.
- `npm run typecheck`, `npm run build`, and `git diff --check` pass.

### Active
- Validate gameplay behavior, especially AI competitiveness and landing/damage/head-win handling.
- Review upgrade progression and repeat chip awards in play; no browser gameplay testing has been reported.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Test the game in-browser, focusing on consecutive bounce stacking/reset, limb-loss order and stamina resistance, head launch/finish crossing, and AI competitiveness.
2. Confirm cleared-course replays still award chips and upgrade progression remains balanced; adjust if needed.

## Relevant Files
- `src/game.ts`: terrain, physics, collision, damage, AI, rendering, race awards.
- `src/main.ts`: upgrade prices, HUD, menus, objectives, and progression.
- `README.md`: controls, features, scope notes, and tuning references.

## Important Context
- Changes are uncommitted; `git status --short` showed modified `README.md` and untracked project files including `src/`, `package.json`, and `package-lock.json`.
- `finishRace()` awards chips from completed objectives on each race, including replays.

messages.summary:
## Objective
- Refine the existing playable Kamikaze Robots remake and validate landing physics, damage/head launch, course difficulty, and upgrade balance.

## Requirements
- Stack bounce power after consecutive feet-first landings following at least one air spin; reset immediately on non-feet-first contact.
- Body-first impacts cause limb loss in arms-first order, with stamina resistance; good landings wear limbs slowly.
- Eject the head on the next contact after losing all four limbs, launching in the body’s current orientation; Explosion scales launch distance/speed, and the head can win by crossing the finish.
- Match terrain colliders to visible ground, including bumps and slopes.
- Lengthen and harden courses while preserving names, visual style, menus, and objectives.
- Slow upgrade progression and keep AI competitive; retain cleared-course chip replays.
- Preserve “HOLD TO BRAKE,” responsive controls, and clear damage/power-reset feedback.

## Decisions
- Continue with the existing TypeScript/Vite project and procedural course system.
- Keep course names and themes; increase course length, terrain variation, and difficulty through the existing level-generation table.
- Interpolate the same 5-unit terrain samples for collision and rendering.
- Upgrade prices: 1 chip for levels 1–2, 2 for 3–5, 3 for 6–8, and 5 thereafter.
- Cleared-course replay chip awards remain repeatable.

## Work State
### Completed
- Increased generated course lengths, slopes, bump counts, and terrain heights.
- Added bounce stacking/reset state, limb wear/loss, and head-launch state and physics.
- Added current-orientation head launch, head rendering, and head-only movement after ejection.
- Aligned terrain drawing and stroke endpoint sampling.
- Added HUD feedback for limb count, bounce multiplier, and power reset.
- Updated `README.md` with controls, features, scope notes, and tuning references.
- Fixed TypeScript issues in `src/game.ts`; previously `npm run typecheck`, `npm run build`, and `git diff --check` passed.
- Adjusted HUD objective checks to use best spin/height, and race position to track head progress when ejected.

### Active
- Validate gameplay, especially bounce stacking/reset, limb-loss sequence and stamina resistance, head launch/finish crossing, and AI competitiveness.
- Re-run typecheck/build after the latest HUD edit; investigate difficulty simulation results.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Run `npm run typecheck`, `npm run build`, and `git diff --check` after the latest `src/main.ts` change.
2. Test gameplay in-browser, focusing on damage, head wins, repeated-course awards, upgrade pacing, and AI competitiveness; tune any failures.

## Relevant Files
- `src/game.ts`: terrain, physics, collision, damage, AI, rendering, race awards.
- `src/main.ts`: upgrade prices, HUD, menus, objectives, and progression.
- `README.md`: controls, features, scope notes, and tuning references.

## Important Context
- Changes are uncommitted; `git status --short` showed modified `README.md` and untracked project files including `src/`, `package.json`, and `package-lock.json`.
- A Node-based gameplay harness (not a browser test) showed the player could finish the first course with automatic braking, but not several later courses; bots also failed to finish in the tested scenarios.
- `finishRace()` awards chips from completed objectives on each race, including replays.

+## Controls
+
+- Hold **Space**, **Down**, **Z**, or press and hold the large on-screen button to brake/reverse your rotation and point the robot's feet down.
+- Let go to free-spin clockwise. More spin earns a stronger bounce. Time your brake before you hit the ground.
+- **Escape** pauses a race; click the on-screen buttons to resume or quit. **S** opens settings from the main menu.
+- Mouse and touch are supported. Sound effects are synthesized locally with Web Audio and can be toggled in-race or in settings.
+
+## Features
+
+- Tournament progression with **30 named, increasingly long and demanding courses**, unlockable in order, and cleared-course replay for chip farming.
+- Quick Race / Practice with solo play or up to three configurable AI bots.
+- Automatic downhill motion, bump and gap terrain, clockwork kick intro, continuous camera follow, airborne spin control, angle-sensitive landings and springy bounce.
+- Progressive damage: arms break first, then legs. If the robot's torso is all that's left, an impact ejects a rocket-powered head that can still cross the finish line.
+- Four race objectives (win, spin, height and distance), up to four chips per race, four purchasable upgrades with visible stat effects, and local save data.
+- Original cartoon robot/terrain illustration, themed hills and space courses, sparks, debris, screen shake, chiptune-style synthesized SFX, HUD, pause, how-to screen and responsive portrait layout.
+
+## Scope notes
+
+- This is an inspired recreation, not a frame-for-frame port. It uses original vector-style art and a shared procedural terrain model; the 30 courses vary in length, challenge settings and visual theme rather than using 30 separately authored track layouts.
+- Quick Race supports solo practice or AI opponents. Local pass-and-play multiplayer is not implemented.
+
+## Tuning
+
+- `src/game.ts`: the `LEVELS` list-generation table, `THEMES`, `ground`, physics (`startJump`, `updateActor`, `badImpact`) and rendering.
+- `src/main.ts`: menus, controls, race HUD, objective thresholds, progression and upgrades.
+- `src/style.css`: interface and responsive styling.
+
+Progress is stored in browser `localStorage` under `kamikaze-save`. Clear the site's storage to reset the tournament.
